This touch of Winter in tho air is altogether sea-

rejoicing that the Summer at last is ended and that

and the heliotropes are backened. Even yet, how
ever some OF the more sturdy plants are struggling
with the coming Winter and the man who keeps
weather record will set down 1877 as the year when

LONDON, August 2, 1871


A correspondent telegraphing from Bull
gareni, fifteen miles east of Plevna, gives a
detailed account Of the fighting of Mon
day. The Turkish force was estimated
at $4,000. They occupied series
of positions which are naturally
strong and also artificially fortified in
every available spot, forming horseshoe in
front Of Plevna with both TANKS resting on
the river vid. The Russian force consisted
Of the Ninth army corps, under General
Brudener; the Thirtieth division and Thir-
tieth brigade Of the Second corps under
Prince Schackesky, with three brigades of
calalry and 100 guns.


THE RUSSIAN PLAN OF ATTACK.


1t was arranged that General Krudener
should attack the Turkish centre at Grivica
and the northern flank of the intrenched
position over Bahova, while Schackesky at
tackled Radizvo, and General Skobeleff, Jr.,
held in check strong Turkish force at
Looca, which was the extremity of the Turk
ish line.


STUBBORN TURKISH DEFENCE.


General Krudener began the battle about
halfpast nine o'clock. After a long bonn
bardment he succeeded in silencing the
Turkish cannon at Grivica, but could never
expel the infantry from the earthworks. He
spent the whole afternoon unavailingly en-
aeavoring to force the northern flank of the
Turkish position, desisting after dark with
out having gained anything material and
having himself suffered considerable loss.


TURKISH FARrHwoRK CARRIED.


Prince Schakosky about noon carried
Radizevo, and, planting four batteries on a
ridge beyond, bombagded the nearest Turk
ish position, which was an earthwork armed
with cannon in front of an intrenched
village. After an hours cannonade he
silenced the Turkish guns, and his infantry,
after long and bloody contest, carried the
earthwork and village.


SECOND TURKISH POSITION CAPTURED


The second Turkish position, consisting
Of redout and series intrenched vine-
yards strongly held, was then attacked and
ultimately carried, but with q terrible effort
and very severe loss, owing to the heavy
Turkish artillery fire.


USELESS SUCCESSES


The Russians, moreover, were unable to
utilize the captured position. About four
o'clock reserve brigade was brought up
and an attack made on the positions imme-
diately covering Plevna The attack con-
tinued till nearly sunset. The Turkish in
fantry was in great force in continuous
line under shelter of trenches.


NO IMPRESSION MADE.


Despite the most stubborn aHorts, no im-
preston could be made upon that line.
Two companies of Russian infantry did
work round to the right of the Turkish
trenches and entered the town of Plevna,
but it was impossible to hold it. The Russian
batteries pushed boldly forward into the
position first taken to attempt to keep down
the Turkish cannonade, which was crashing
into the infantry in the open field, but they
were compelled soon to evacuate the hazard
Gus spot.


THE TURK. ASSUME THE OFFENSIVE.


At shutdown the Turks made continuous
forward movement and reoccupied their
second position. The Russian infantry
made succession of desperate stands and
died like heroes The Turks gradually re-
took everything they had lost. The fighting
lasted long after nighttall.


BAsHI-BAzooKs KILL THE WOUNDED.


With the darkness the bashi-bazouks took
possession Of the battlefield and slew all
the wounded. The Russians held the
heights above Radizeoo, but the bashi-
bazouks worked around to their rear and
fell on the wounded collected in the village
of Radizeoo.

An enormous quantity of rain has fallen
during the past week over the watersheds
of the rivers between the Atlantic coast and
the Missouri. But in the western country

fore the flow of the water from the surround

In the Ohio Valley, however, MS we'll as

ers it rather better authority than any

loaded hifalutin, she rarely reads
Views are of no importance in her estl-

tice of reading it, because she thinks she

paper down with an air of disappoint-
ment, and half contemptuous gesture,

Coldly and bright draws in the day;
Gloomy and drear it steals away;
For slow Y now comes up the sun,
His summers ardent labors done;
And low his golden wheel declines
Where winter shows his starry signs.
No more to earth the fervid beams
Give beauty such as poet dreams:
No more descends the glorious ray,
The rapture of the summer day.
The sky's deep blue is waxing pale,
The suns inspiring fervors fail;
The slantng beam he gives is chill
Within the vale and on the hill
And now with many jealous fold,
The clouds would all his cheer withhold,
Nor would on plain or height bestow
The soothing of his waning glow.
The flowers are gone, save those that still,
Like friends who cleave to us through ill,
Outbrave the bitter wind that blows,
And deck their season to its close.
The leaves that late were only stirred
By gentlest breath, that only heard
The song birds note, round these the blast
Blows keen and fierce, and rude and fast
The rising gale filings far and wide
Their withered bloom and idle pride.
The birds have fed; the wind alone
Makes song in many sullen tone.
But sudden through the bursting sky
The sun again comes out on high;
The clouds fall back to yield him way,
And fly before his eager r.y;
And gladness fills the breast amain-
The glimpse of summer come again!
All sweet the beam, but like the smile
With which the dying would beguile
The mourning heart-the last sad ray
Love gives to cheer our tears away.
The light is gone, the moments bloom
Is sunk again in cold and gloom.
So pass away all things of earth,
Whate'er we prize of love and worth
The form once dear; the voice that cheered (;
The friends by many tie endeared;
The dreams the aching heart forgets;
The hopes that fade in cold regrets.
Sweet scenes, dear haunts that once l knew,
My heart yet fondy turns to you.
Let seasons change, and be ye bright
With all the summer-tides delight,
Or let the winters gloom be yours,
Your beauty still for me endures;
For memory keeps unfaded yey
What Love would have me not forget

English versus American Football.


In the recent football match between Yale
and Princeton the working OF the new Rugby
rules came out in sharp contrast with the old
fashioned style, and not always in favor Of
the former. Now and then there were most
excited and determined rushes, pretty
dashes and duckings, and, for minute, the
spectator was admirably entertained. But
then there would come q pause, one man
would get the ball and place it on the
ground, many more would bunch around
him. all STOPPING low, and then for long in
terval the game seemed at dead standstill,
no one doing anything at all. Whenever the
ball got over the side line of the field,
thus producing 'foul," there was more
delay, so that the untechnical spectator
could not tell whether the game was over or
not Under the new rules, too, instead OF win
ming victory by kicking the ball anywhere
over the long line forming the end Of the
field at the enemy's rear, it must be sent
between two standards and over q bar
scarcely longer than gymnast's horizontal
bar--a feat that would seem we'll nigh i'm
possible where there are SO many on side.
As between all this fnesse and dull delay
and the good old American game, where
from beginning to end it Was one unceasng
desperate struggle, man after man falling
out exhausted and the stayers winning the
fight, it seems to us that little has been
gained by the innovation. Alertness, dash,
feetness and intrepidity-theso qualities
this admirable pastime begets in greater
degree than any other game except, per-
haps. polo. But why not have also stay-a
quality almost as valuable as all the rest
together? Under the American rules the
winners must have it; under the Rugby
rules, as played by Yale and Princeton, it
seems to be entirely unnecessary.

LADY FLORA BECOMES CATHOLIC.


After the death of her mother Lady Flora
went to bennington Hall, the residence Of
the notorious young Lord Hastings. whose
career had been ended and his death
hastened by dissipation. When this noble
old mansion was dismantled to pay the debts
of the unfortunate lord Lady Flora went to
the Island of Butte to stay with her cousin,
Lord Butte, and while there she formed the
resolution to enter the Catholic Church.
She was received in due time by Monseigneur
Capel.


PERSECUTION WINS A CoRoNEr.
Her family Immediately began to perse-
cute her. The trials she suffered owing to
the attitude assumed by her father threw
her under the protection of the Duchess of
Norfolk, who claimed marriage relation
ship through Lady Butte. the daughter Of
Lord Howard, brother of the present Duke
of Norfolk. Out Of this protection grew the
happy alliance formed yesterday at the Ora
tory. 1t is said the young lady's heart was
captured long before the Duke asked her
hand.


PERSONAL QUALITIES.


She possesses nothing in the way of per-
sonal beauty, though her whole appearance.
height and general department betray her
high origin. Like the Duke. she has no
special literary taste or culture, but she has
inherited the warm heart and good practi-
cal judgment of her mother. She is sin
cere, simple hearted woman.


MARn1AaEABLE YOUNG LADIES DISAPPOINTED.


While her relatives must concede the brill
fancy Of her match, despite her apostacy
from the Protestant Church, several noble
families of old Catholics are offended at her
being selected as o wife by the wealthy
Duke It was rumored at one time that the
Dukes affections were in another quarter !;
in fact, he has been openly admired by
mothers having marriageable daughters.
But the present alliance can scarcely give
rise to any scandal, notwithstanding the
prevailing undertone Of indignation.


SCENE IN THE oRAToRY


When the gas in the chapel was turned
up, after an interval of partial darkness, the
scene was striking. The organ pealed forth
a wedding march. especially composed for
the occasion, and the acolytes marched into
the space within the rails of the altar The
altar was brilliantly lit up. A coup d@il
over the assembled congregation discovered
some Of the wealthiest and most influential
personages in Great Britain. Most of the
titled ladies wore the proverbial black silk,
but there were enough bright headdresses,
flowing colored ribbons and shining, scin-
tillating diamonds to relieve the monotony
occasioned by the prevalence of black.
Rich perfumes pervaded the chapel during
the entire ceremonial.


PROMINENT LADIES PRESENT.


Prominent among the ladies present were
the Marchioness of Butte; Lady Ermyn-
troude Russell, daughter of the Duke OF
Bedford; Lady Maud Grinston, Lady Dud-
ley Stanhope, Lady Ripon and Miss Kir-
wan.


THE OFFICIATING BISHOPS.


The Bishops of Southwark, Nottingham
and Port Louis officiated, the former inton-
ing the first portion of the impressive cere-
mony.


BRIDESMAIDS.


The bridesmaids were Lady Egidia Hast
ings, sister of the bride; Ladies' Anna How
ard and Margaret Howard, Misses Minna
Hope, Josephine Hope and Theresa Hope,
nieces of the Duke; Lady Grinston, Lady
Adelaide Forbes and Miss Clinton, cousins
of the bride; Miss Alice Howard, cousin Of
the Duke; Lady Ermyntroude Russell and
the brides cousin, Miss Kirwan.


HOW THEY WERE DRESSED.


All the bridesmaids wore dresses mado of
ivory poult de sole, draped ivory broche
trimmed with cardinal velvet. Rubens hats
trimmed with cardinal velvet and cream
colored and cardinal feathers. Each brides
maid also wore gold bracelets studded with
pearls and ornamentcd with monogram OF
the Duke and Duchess in pearls and
diamonds, surmounted with coronets in
diamonds. These were presents from the
bridegroom.


THE DUCHESS TRAVELLING COSTUME.


The brides travelling costume was superb.
It consisted of robe of sapphire Lyons

pean nations beheld Mr. Hayes

tered to him by the Chief Justice, they had

iment has not failed in the United States,
